title: The Slow Vow
premise: Lior Ravensworth has spent seven years raising his daughter Wren alone and keeping the past sealed behind the counter of his bookshop. When a water-damaged letter postmarked eleven years ago surfaces in a donated box of books — a letter he wrote and never sent to Marisol Vane, the woman who left town to honor her family's duty — it forces him to relive the night everything broke. As Marisol returns to settle her late mother's estate, the two are drawn together by the letter, Wren's quiet hope for a family, and a town that never stopped rooting for them. But forgiving each other proves easier than forgiving himself, and when Marisol receives an offer that would take her away again, Lior must finally choose love over the safety of small steps. In the end, he sends a new letter — hand-delivered — and they build a life measured not in safe steps but in shared ones.
about_author: Paloma Galloway is a former small-town librarian who writes romances about second chances, stubborn hearts, and the places that hold us together. She lives in a coastal village with her partner, two cats, and an ever-losing battle against her to-be-read shelf.

chapters.title: The Weight of Ordinary Days
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A morning in the bookshop: opening the shutters, Wren's school run, the comfortable rhythm of seven careful years. He tells himself he is content. Emotional beat: the fragile peace that precedes disruption.

chapters.title: A Box of Someone Else's Past
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A donation of books from the estate sale of Edith Vane arrives; tucked inside one is a water-stained letter, postmarked eleven years ago, in Lior's own handwriting — addressed to Marisol and never sent. Emotional beat: shock; the past knocking loudly.

chapters.title: What the Letter Said
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, flashback woven through present. He rereads his younger self's words — a plea for Marisol to stay, written the night she left to care for her dying mother. He burns nothing; he hides the letter instead. Emotional beat: shame resurfacing.

chapters.title: Wren Asks About the Sea
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (age nine). She notices her father reading an old letter at midnight and asks, innocently, whether she ever had another family besides him. Emotional beat: tenderness and dread entwined.

chapters.title: The Estate Sale
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She returns to Harborlight to settle her mother's affairs, planning a two-week stay, no longer. She walks past the bookshop twice before daring to look through the glass. Emotional beat: homesickness for a place that hurt her.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Small Talk
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Marisol comes into the shop under the pretense of buying a novel. Their conversation is polite, brittle, full of unsaid things. Wren appears and offers her a bookmark. Emotional beat: longing disguised as courtesy.

chapters.title: The Town That Remembers
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Old friends — the baker, the librarian, Wren's teacher — welcome her back with warmth and pointed questions about 'that Ravensworth boy.' She learns how Lior rebuilt his life alone. Emotional beat: found family tightening its circle.

chapters.title: Rain on the Awning
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A storm traps them both under the shop awning after closing. The first honest exchange in eleven years: apologies shaped like weather talk. He almost mentions the letter; he doesn't. Emotional beat: proximity without confession.

chapters.title: Duty's Long Shadow
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Sorting her mother's papers, she finds evidence Edith knew about Lior's letter — and hid it from her. Grief curdles into anger at everyone, including herself. Emotional beat: betrayal reframing the past.

chapters.title: Pancakes and Confessions
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Marisol joins their Sunday breakfast 'by accident.' Wren, sharp-eyed, begins scheming quietly, leaving books about lighthouses and second chances on the counter. Emotional beat: a child's hope doing what adults cannot.

chapters.title: The Letter Goes Missing
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The hidden letter disappears from the shop's back room. Panic: did Marisol find it? Did Wren? Rising tension as he tears the shop apart. Emotional beat: fear that truth will arrive uncontrolled.

chapters.title: What Wren Read
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She took the letter, unable to stop reading. She confronts her father gently: 'Why didn't you send it?' Lior admits he was afraid — of rejection, of being enough, of wanting too much. Emotional beat: the mirror moment; self-forgiveness begins.

chapters.title: Harborlight Festival
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The town's lantern festival pulls everyone into the square. Lior and Marisol dance, almost kiss, and are interrupted by a phone call: Marisol's job offer abroad, effective within the month. Emotional beat: joy undercut by the ticking clock.

chapters.title: Two Weeks Becomes One
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She extends her stay, then learns the estate must be settled fast and the offer won't wait. She and Lior fall into something real — shared coffees, repaired shelves, Wren's laughter — while both pretend there's time. Emotional beat: love against duty, first collision.

chapters.title: The Argument in the Back Room
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Marisol finds proof Lior had the letter all along and never told her. The fight is fierce: eleven years of silence blamed back and forth. She leaves; Wren cries; Lior sits among broken shelving. Emotional beat: climax of old wounds.

chapters.title: The Person in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Rock bottom. His sister-in-choice, the baker Rosa, forces him to say aloud what he's avoided: he punished himself for Marisol's leaving long after she stopped blaming him. He writes a new letter — this time meaning every word. Emotional beat: self-forgiveness achieved.

chapters.title: Empty Dock at Dawn
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Packed to leave, she reads Edith's final unsent letter to her — her mother's own regret over choosing duty over love. Marisol understands at last where the pattern came from, and refuses to repeat it. Emotional beat: breaking the inheritance of silence.

chapters.title: Hand-Delivered
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. He catches her at the ferry dock and does not hand her the letter — he reads it aloud, voice shaking, in front of gulls and strangers. It ends: 'I am not asking you to stay. I am asking you to come home.' Emotional beat: vulnerability as courage.

chapters.title: The Ferry That Waited
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The ferry horn sounds. She boards — then steps off at the last second, choosing Harborlight, choosing them, on her own terms and timeline. Emotional beat: agency reclaimed; love chosen freely.

chapters.title: Three Signatures
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Practical magic: Marisol declines the offer, takes over Edith's house, and signs a lease to open a tea room beside the bookshop, connecting their doors. Wren draws the three of them as lighthouses. Emotional beat: found family made official.

chapters.title: The Slow Vow
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. No grand wedding — instead, a quiet evening ceremony in the shop after hours, witnessed by the whole town, vows written slowly and read slowly, because they mean them. Emotional beat: love as a promise kept daily.

chapters.title: Measured in Shared Steps
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. One year later: the connected shops thrive, a new letter framed behind the counter next to the old one, and Wren writes a letter of her own — to the future. Emotional beat: peace earned, memory honored, story complete.
